blocks.text: An infusion pump is an electronic or mechanical medical device that delivers fluids, medications or other prescribed solutions into a patient at a controlled rate.
It is particularly important in pediatrics and neonatology, where small errors in infusion volume or rate can cause serious harm.
OSCE objective: You should be able to identify the pump, distinguish its types, explain its components, program a prescribed infusion, respond to alarms and discuss medication safety.

items.text: Name: Infusion pump.
Classification: Medical fluid-delivery device.
Primary function: Controlled administration of prescribed fluids or medications.
Common settings: Emergency departments, wards, operating theatres, intensive care units and neonatal units.

blocks.text: A. Volumetric infusion pump
Delivers fluid from an IV bag through compatible administration tubing. Commonly used for IV fluids, antibiotics and other infusions.
B. Syringe pump
Uses a motor-driven mechanism to push the plunger of a syringe at a controlled rate. Useful for low-volume infusions and potent medications.
C. Ambulatory infusion pump
A portable device that allows selected infusions to continue while a patient moves around or receives care outside hospital.
D. Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) pump
Allows a patient to request prescribed analgesic doses within programmed limits. It incorporates safety settings such as lockout intervals.
Exam distinction: A syringe pump is a type of infusion pump. A volumetric pump typically uses a dedicated administration set, whereas a syringe pump uses a compatible syringe.

items.text: Controlled IV fluid administration: When an accurate delivery rate is required.
Antibiotic infusions: To administer prescribed doses over a specified duration.
Vasoactive medication: For example, noradrenaline in a suitably monitored critical-care setting.
Insulin infusions: When prescribed and delivered according to the relevant protocol.
Analgesia and sedation: Including selected opioid, sedative and anaesthetic infusions.
Neonatal and pediatric therapy: For accurate delivery of small fluid volumes and medication doses.
Chemotherapy: With appropriate validated equipment and drug-specific precautions.
Parenteral nutrition: To deliver prescribed nutritional solutions at a controlled rate.

blocks.text: Not every pump is suitable for every medication or route. The device, administration set, syringe, drug concentration and programmed parameters must all be compatible.
1. Display screen
Shows the programmed rate, volume to be infused (VTBI), volume delivered, remaining time and alarm messages, depending on the model.
2. Control panel or keypad
Allows the clinician to enter and modify infusion parameters and operate the device.
3. Pumping mechanism
Moves fluid through the administration set at the programmed rate. The mechanism differs between volumetric and syringe pumps.
4. Sensors
Depending on the model, detect air in the line, downstream pressure, fluid flow or other conditions that may require an alarm.
5. Alarm system
Alerts the user to detected problems such as occlusion, air in the line, low battery or an infusion nearing completion.
6. Power supply and battery
Provides electrical power and, in many models, temporary operation during transport or power interruption.
7. Pole clamp or mounting system
Secures the pump to a suitable IV pole or mounting rail.
Other features may include a drug library, dose-error reduction software, a bolus function and a lockable keypad.

items.text: More accurate and consistent delivery than ordinary gravity infusion when correctly configured.
Allows precise programming of infusion rates and volumes.
Useful for medications with narrow therapeutic margins.
Supports low-volume infusion in neonates and children.
Many models have alarms and safety features.
Reduces the need for continuous manual adjustment of a roller clamp.
Some models support dose-based programming and drug libraries.

blocks.text: Important limitation: A pump can still deliver the wrong medication or dose if the clinician enters incorrect parameters, uses an incompatible set or fails to recognize a device malfunction.

items.text: Requires electricity or a sufficiently charged battery.
More expensive than gravity infusion.
Requires training and familiarity with the particular model.
Incorrect programming can result in serious dosing errors.
Occlusion may interrupt medication delivery.
Some pumps may allow a post-occlusion bolus when an obstruction is released, depending on the device and circumstances.
Air detection and other safety features are not infallible.
Mechanical failure, sensor faults or incorrect loading can affect performance.
Alarms may be missed or incorrectly silenced.
Certain pumps require dedicated consumables or administration sets.

blocks.title: Before operating the pump, explain that you would:

items.text: Perform hand hygiene and identify the patient correctly.
Check the prescription, medication, dose, route, concentration and intended duration.
Confirm allergies and relevant patient-specific considerations.
Inspect the medication container, syringe or infusion bag.
Verify that the pump is appropriate for the prescribed therapy and that its service checks are current.
Check the power supply and battery status.
Select a compatible administration set or syringe.
Prime the line according to the manufacturer's instructions before connecting it to the patient.
Inspect the tubing for air, leaks, kinks and damage.
Check the IV access site and ensure connections are secure.
Program the prescribed rate and VTBI, or the correct dose parameters if the pump supports dose-based programming.
Independently double-check high-alert medication settings when required by local policy.
Confirm the displayed settings before starting the infusion.

blocks.text: For medications such as insulin, heparin and vasoactive infusions, use the applicable drug-specific protocol and required independent checks.

subsections.subsection_title: 7. How to use an infusion pump — OSCE demonstration

blocks.text: The exact buttons and loading sequence differ by manufacturer. In the exam, describe the general procedure and demonstrate using the particular model supplied.
Step 1 — Verify the prescription
Confirm the patient, prescribed fluid or medication, concentration, route, rate, volume and duration.
Step 2 — Inspect the device
Check the pump's condition, service status, power supply and battery. Ensure it is mounted securely.
Step 3 — Load the administration set
Use the correct compatible set and follow the manufacturer's loading instructions. Ensure the tubing is correctly seated and any required clamps are positioned appropriately.
Step 4 — Prime the line
Remove air from the tubing before patient connection. Follow the device instructions and maintain aseptic technique.
Step 5 — Enter the prescribed settings
Enter the required rate and VTBI, or the correct dose-based parameters. Confirm units carefully, such as mL/h versus mg/h.
Step 6 — Perform the safety check
Compare the screen against the prescription and medication label. Check concentration, units, patient weight if relevant, rate, VTBI and any required drug-library selection.
Step 7 — Connect and commence infusion
Assess the IV access, disinfect the needleless connector and allow it to dry. Connect aseptically, then start the infusion as prescribed.
Step 8 — Monitor the infusion
Confirm that the pump is running without alarms, the rate is correct and the patient is tolerating therapy. Inspect the IV site and reassess according to the medication and patient's condition.

content_groups.group_title: How to calculate the pump rate

blocks.text: For a standard volume-based infusion:
Example: Administer 250 mL over 2 hours.
Program the pump to 125 mL/h, with the appropriate VTBI and other settings required by that model.

For a dose-based infusion, additional information is needed, such as the prescribed dose, patient's weight when applicable, and medication concentration. Never calculate a dose-based rate from volume alone.
There is no universal absolute contraindication to an infusion pump. The device must be appropriate for the intended medication, patient and clinical circumstances.

Assess the patient and inspect the line and access site; do not force a flush
Stop the infusion as indicated and clear the air according to the manufacturer's procedure before restarting
Connect to a safe power supply and ensure uninterrupted treatment where necessary
Verify the treatment plan and next step
Incorrectly loaded tubing or open pump door

Empty bag, closed clamp or obstructed tubing upstream
Inspect the container, tubing and clamps

blocks.text: Not all pumps have the same sensors or alarm messages. Always interpret the actual alarm on the device.

items.text: Medication overdose or underdose.
Interruption of critical medication delivery.
Infiltration, extravasation or phlebitis.
Infection due to poor aseptic technique.
Fluid overload.
Air entry or air embolism.
Delay in therapy from an unrecognized alarm.
Post-occlusion bolus in susceptible setups.

blocks.text: Examiner's rule: Never simply silence an alarm and walk away. Assess the patient first, identify and correct the cause safely, and escalate when required.
The pump is not a diagnostic instrument. You assess its operational status and the patient's response.
Normal operation

items.text: Correct programmed rate and VTBI.
Infusion is running as intended.
No unresolved alarms or visible tubing problems.
Secure connections and a satisfactory IV site.
Patient remains clinically stable or improves as expected.

blocks.text: Abnormal operation

items.text: Unexpected alarm or interrupted delivery.
Incorrect displayed parameters.
Unexpected volume delivered or discrepancy in the remaining volume.
Leakage, swelling or pain at the IV site.
New deterioration, breathlessness or signs of medication toxicity.

blocks.text: This is one of the highest-yield sections for pediatric OSCEs.

items.text: Weight-based dosing: Verify the current weight and units, and calculate medication doses using the relevant protocol.
Small fluid volumes: Use an appropriate pump where precise, low-volume delivery is required.
Drug concentration: Confirm the prepared concentration before programming dose-based infusions.
Dose-error reduction software: Use the appropriate drug library when available and indicated.
High-alert medications: Follow independent double-check policies for medications such as insulin and vasoactive agents.
Line dead space: In neonates, fluid and medication in the tubing can significantly affect delivery time and the timing of dose changes.
Flushes: Unplanned flushing of a line containing medication can deliver an unintended bolus. Follow neonatal line-management protocols.
Occlusion alarms: Small cannulas and narrow tubing may occlude more readily; promptly investigate alarms.
Monitoring: Monitor clinical status, fluid balance, infusion site and relevant physiological or laboratory parameters.
Caregiver safety: Ensure tubing is secured and that movement does not pull on the cannula or compromise the infusion.

blocks.text: Important: An infusion pump improves control of delivery but does not make an incorrect prescription, calculation or medication concentration safe.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. Common OSCE questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is an infusion pump?
A medical device that delivers prescribed fluids or medications at a controlled rate.
Q2. Differentiate a volumetric pump from a syringe pump.
A volumetric pump generally delivers fluid through a compatible administration set, while a syringe pump uses a motor-driven mechanism to advance a syringe plunger.
Q3. What is VTBI?
Volume to be infused: the volume the pump is programmed to deliver before the set volume target is reached.
Q4. What would you do if the pump alarmed for occlusion?
Assess the patient, check the tubing and cannula site for kinks, closed clamps, obstruction or infiltration, and follow the manufacturer's instructions. I would not force fluid through the line.
Q5. Why is an infusion pump important in neonates?
It permits controlled administration of small volumes and medication rates, reducing the risk of unintended rapid or excessive delivery when used correctly.
Q6. Does an infusion pump eliminate medication errors?
No. Incorrect prescriptions, wrong concentrations, wrong programming, incompatible equipment and failure to respond to alarms can still cause errors.
Q7. Why should the line be primed before connecting it to the patient?
To fill the tubing and remove air before patient connection, while maintaining aseptic technique.
Q8. What is a drug library?
A database of medication-specific parameters and dosing limits used by compatible pumps to support safer programming.
Q9. What is a potential consequence of releasing an occlusion?
Some pump setups can deliver accumulated pressure-related fluid as a post-occlusion bolus. The risk depends on the device, tubing, medication and circumstances.
Q10. What do you do if the power fails during a critical infusion?
Assess the patient and the status of the infusion immediately, use an approved backup power source or suitable replacement device, and escalate promptly to prevent interruption of essential therapy.

items.text: Programming the wrong units, such as mg/h instead of mL/h.
Using the wrong patient's weight.
Entering the wrong medication concentration.
Failing to prime the line before connecting it.
Using incompatible tubing or a syringe.
Forgetting to enter or verify the VTBI.
Ignoring an occlusion or air-in-line alarm.
Silencing an alarm without investigating its cause.
Failing to inspect the cannula site.
Assuming that a running pump guarantees correct drug delivery.

blocks.text: Examiner tip: If asked to demonstrate the pump, narrate the safety checks and verify the programmed settings aloud. If an unfamiliar model is presented, explain that you would follow the manufacturer's instructions rather than guess the button sequence.
